headline: Saudi Warehousing and Logistics Expo opens in Riyadh with 350 exhibitors
deck: The Vice Minister of Transport opened the third edition at RICEC, where 350 exhibitors from more than 25 countries are showing to a market the ministry wants read as a global hub.
excerpt: The third Saudi Warehousing and Logistics Expo opened in Riyadh on 8 September, inaugurated by the Vice Minister of Transport and Logistic Services with more than 350 exhibiting companies from over 25 countries on the floor.
content:
The third Saudi Warehousing and Logistics Expo opened at the Riyadh International Convention and Exhibition Centre on 8 September, inaugurated by Dr Rumaih bin Mohammed Al-Rumaih, Vice Minister of Transport and Logistic Services, deputising for the minister and the show's patron, Eng. Saleh bin Nasser Al-Jasser.

More than 350 exhibiting companies from over 25 countries are showing upwards of 4,000 products and services across the three days, according to figures given at the opening and carried by the Saudi Press Agency. The country count is the more telling of the two numbers: it is higher than the organiser's pre-show material indicated, and it is the metric that separates a domestic trade fair from one that importers and international suppliers treat as worth the flight.

Ministerial patronage is not decoration at an event like this. The Ministry of Transport and Logistic Services is the body that licenses logistics operators, designates logistics zones and sets the terms on which foreign operators can hold Saudi warehousing assets. Its presence at the opening is read by exhibitors as a signal about the direction of that licensing pipeline, which is why the deputising minister's remarks — framed around the Kingdom's ambition to establish itself as a global logistics hub and a link in international trade — matter more to the floor than the usual opening-ceremony language.

A summit ran alongside the exhibition on the opening day, with panels drawn from the ministry, the Federation of Saudi Chambers, DHL Global Forwarding Saudi Arabia, Morph Logistics Solutions and Caden Investment. The published agenda covered infrastructure and investment, multimodal connectivity, warehousing and distribution, digital resilience, supply chain security and trade facilitation. No individual speakers were named in the coverage of those sessions, only the participating organisations.

The market figures circulating at the show come from the organiser, dmg events, rather than from the ministry, and are worth attributing carefully. They put the Saudi commercial vehicle market at $6.7bn, project the e-commerce logistics segment to double by 2027, and state that 25 of 42 planned logistics hubs are now operational. That last figure is the one with the most weight behind it, and the one this publication examines separately.

Exhibitor names released before the show include SAL Logistics, Almajdouie and the automation suppliers Swisslog, SSI Schäfer and Kardex. Transliterations of several Saudi exhibitor names differ between the Arabic and English releases, so the official floor list is the authority.

No contracts, memoranda of understanding or product launches had been announced at the show as of its final day. Audited attendance figures have not been published; the 18,000-visitor number in circulation remains a projection. The exhibition closes on 10 September.
